title: Similarity-Augmented System-One Decision Models for Patient Triage: A Framework Unifying Fast Probabilistic Decision Models and Patient Similarity Networks
content: Triage is a constrained, high-frequency clinical decision: at the moment of first contact, a patient must be assigned an urgency level and a disposition lane under time pressure. Two recent lines of work address this decision from opposite directions. System-One decision models, exemplified by JEV and its open medical variant MedJev, answer typed questions (a choice among options, an ordinal score, or the probability of a binary event) about a patient state in a single forward pass, returning calibrated probabilities without generating text; they match or exceed supervised models on physiologic outcomes such as in-hospital mortality but underperform them on operational outcomes such as emergency department (ED) admission, which depend on institution-specific practice patterns that a zero-shot model cannot know. Patient similarity networks, in contrast, encode local practice implicitly: patients are nodes, edges are feature similarities, and graph neural networks (GNNs) over these networks classify triage acuity with high accuracy. Here we unify the two paradigms. We present SimJev, an open-source framework in which a patient similarity network built over a historical cohort supplies a local-practice prior to a System-One decision model through two mechanisms: (i) neighborhood-augmented states, in which the outcome summary of the \(k\) most similar historical patients is injected into the model's input state, and (ii) log-odds fusion, in which the model probability and the similarity-network probability are combined with a weight fit on 50–200 labeled local examples. The framework additionally implements the full GNN node-classification pipeline (GCN, GATv2, GraphSAGE) as a head-to-head comparator. On a public triage cohort of 6,552 patient encounters, the GraphSAGE arm outperforms the \(k\)-nearest-neighbor similarity prior (AUROC 0.984 vs. 0.932; AUPRC 0.686 vs. 0.366), and fusing the GNN probability with a decision-model probability improves calibration (ECE 0.028 to 0.007) without loss of discrimination. We then evaluate the framework end-to-end against a real, locally served open System-One backend (OpenJev 0.1 serving DiffusionGemma-26B) on the same cohort, with a solo-read protocol, two state encodings, and a field-attribution probe, and obtain four findings. First, the zero-shot admission probability is not merely uninformative but unstable in sign: the same frozen model, asked the same question about the same patients, is informative when two categorical fields are absent from its state (AUROC 0.653, 95% CI 0.567–0.737), anti-informative when those fields are present as arbitrary integer codes (0.397, 0.322–0.485), and chance-level when they are present as semantic strings (0.474, 0.386–0.549). Second, the probe localizes two mechanisms: co-asking questions in one request contaminates the answers — the admission question drops from 0.638 asked alone to 0.401 inside a three-question panel, consistent with joint denoising coupling the answer slots — and replacing integer codes with semantic strings removes the anti-informative signal (0.360 to 0.531 within run). Third, neighborhood-augmented states are robust across every configuration tested (AUROC 0.785–0.919), perform best under semantic encoding (0.915), and an echo-control ablation — each patient receiving a random other patient's neighborhood block — collapses performance to chance, establishing that the model genuinely conditions on block content. Fourth, log-odds fusion degrades gracefully in every regime: against anti-informative, contaminated, and chance-level model components the fitted weight falls to zero and the fused arm matches the prior (AUROC 0.917–0.919, ECE 0.004); we find no discrimination gain over the prior and report a borderline trend observed in one configuration (+0.022, \(p \approx 0.06\)) as unconfirmed. We state the scope of these claims explicitly: on a single public cohort, the framework demonstrates feasibility, calibration transfer, and a mechanism-of-action result — the similarity prior is the active ingredient of the augmented decision model — and, as its methodological contribution, that single-pass probability readouts require state-encoding, question-composition, and phrasing ablations as standard practice; discrimination headroom over the prior on credentialed MIMIC-IV-ED data remains the endpoint of the companion study. We release the framework, including the evaluation harness, the OpenJev wire-API integration, the field-attribution probe, the fine-tuning recipe, the synthetic-data mode, and all augmentation mechanisms, as open source.
